title: Why the Federal Minimum Wage Has Lost So Much Purchasing Power

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: Imagine working under a wage floor set over a decade ago. The U.S. federal minimum wage reached $7.25 per hour back in July 2009.

segments.label: scene 2 (compare)
segments.text: From July 2009 to October 2026, the total legal increase for baseline workers was +0%.

segments.label: scene 3 (gauge)
segments.text: This marks an unprecedented wage freeze. In October 2026, the federal rate remains stuck at $7.25 per hour.

segments.label: scene 4 (line)
segments.text: While the minimum wage stood still, typical earnings kept rising. Average hourly pay for non-managers reached $32.75 in October 2026.

segments.label: scene 5 (multiline)
segments.text: Looking at pay growth since July 2009, average worker pay climbed significantly while minimum wage recorded +0% growth.

segments.label: scene 6 (statement)
segments.text: Living costs also expanded, punctuated by an earlier spike in June 2022 when annual consumer price growth hit +9%.

segments.label: scene 7 (kpi)
segments.text: Over the last year from October 2025 to October 2026, minimum wage growth was +0.0%. The federal floor remains frozen.

segments.label: scene 8 (counter)
segments.text: To understand how the federal floor separated from typical worker pay, we turn to January 1970, according to data from the U.S. Department of Labor. Back then, the federal minimum wage was $1.60 per hour.

segments.label: scene 9 (counter)
segments.text: During that same month in January 1970, average hourly pay for non-managerial workers was $3.31.

segments.label: scene 10 (statement)
segments.text: At this baseline, minimum earnings sat much closer to what typical workers brought home each hour.

segments.label: scene 11 (line)
segments.text: Between January 1970 and October 2026, the statutory federal minimum wage recorded a cumulative rise of +353%.

segments.label: scene 12 (line)
segments.text: That overall growth means the October 2026 value is 4.5 times the January 1970 value.

segments.label: scene 13 (bars)
segments.text: Over that exact same timeframe, average hourly pay grew far faster, achieving a +889% total increase.

segments.label: scene 14 (multiline)
segments.text: Mapping both trajectories since 1970 reveals how the baseline minimum wage gradually lost pace with general wage expansion.

segments.label: scene 15 (statement)
segments.text: Wage growth alone doesn't tell the full story. The true test of a minimum wage is its real purchasing power against everyday expenses.

segments.label: scene 16 (counter)
segments.text: Between January 1970 and October 2026, consumer prices exploded by +790%, drastically altering the cost of living.

segments.label: scene 17 (line)
segments.text: That overall expansion means the October 2026 price level sits at 8.9 times its January 1970 baseline value.

segments.label: scene 18 (bars)
segments.text: Look at how pay rules lagged behind. Since January 1980, consumer prices climbed +333%, while the federal minimum wage rose just +134%.

segments.label: scene 19 (line)
segments.text: That erosion accelerated in recent years. From January 2020 to October 2026 alone, consumer prices spiked by another +30%.

segments.label: scene 20 (heatmap)
segments.text: Even looking over the last year from November 2025 to October 2026, consumer prices added an additional +3.8%.

segments.label: scene 21 (multiline)
segments.text: While price tags keep climbing across the country, a static statutory floor forces minimum wage workers to stretch every dollar significantly further.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Why does the federal baseline lag so drastically behind overall economic growth? Unlike indexed social programs, changing this legal floor requires explicit statutory action by Congress.

segments.label: scene 23 (line)
segments.text: Without automatic cost-of-living adjustments, consumer prices expanded by +55% between January 2010 and October 2026.

segments.label: scene 24 (statement)
segments.text: Because statutory pay rules lack built-in inflation triggers, purchasing power quietly erodes whenever prices rise.

segments.label: scene 25 (compare)
segments.text: Meanwhile, market pay continued moving upward. Average hourly earnings for non-managerial workers jumped +73% over that same timeframe since January 2010.

segments.label: scene 26 (line)
segments.text: Looking back at January 2020, average pay stood at $23.91 per hour before surging another +37% through October 2026.

segments.label: scene 27 (bars)
segments.text: Since 2010, average hourly pay surged +73% while the federal minimum wage recorded +0% change, widening the economic rift.

segments.label: scene 28 (kpi)
segments.text: Even over the last year, average hourly earnings climbed +3.3%, while the statutory federal floor remained unchanged.

segments.label: scene 29 (statement)
segments.text: To see how these trends affect everyday life, we must look at household budgets after 2020. Rapidly rising bills created severe real-world challenges for working families across the country.

segments.label: scene 30 (counter)
segments.text: Looking back at January 2010, average non-managerial pay was $18.88 per hour. Over subsequent years, market compensation for typical employees continued expanding steadily.

segments.label: scene 31 (counter)
segments.text: By October 2026, typical worker earnings reached $32.75 per hour, 9.9 times their January 1970 level. General market pay kept compounding over decades.

segments.label: scene 32 (multiline)
segments.text: Since January 2020, average hourly pay rose +37% while consumer prices increased +30%, eroding real wage gains for ordinary households.

segments.label: scene 33 (line)
segments.text: Since January 2015, overall consumer prices climbed +44%, continuously raising the minimum income required to cover essential daily expenses.

segments.label: scene 34 (counter)
segments.text: Market pay climbed to $20.80 in January 2015, pulling typical compensation well beyond statutory wage floors.

segments.label: scene 35 (statement)
segments.text: For workers trapped at the unchanged federal baseline, inflation steadily shrinks purchasing power, forcing families to squeeze every single dollar just to cover basic needs.

segments.label: scene 36 (counter)
segments.text: Decades of steady inflation have fundamentally reshaped the true purchasing power of low-wage workers. Since January 1975, overall consumer prices jumped by +545%.

segments.label: scene 37 (line)
segments.text: At the same time, policy inertia kept federal minimum pay static, showing zero upward movement since July 2009.

segments.label: scene 38 (slope)
segments.text: By contrast, broader labor markets moved forward. Back in January 2000, statutory floor pay sat at $5.15 while average non-managerial compensation was $13.74.

segments.label: scene 39 (statement)
segments.text: Because the statutory floor lacks automatic inflation indexing, price spikes permanently shrink what entry-level pay can purchase.

segments.label: scene 40 (slope)
segments.text: The long-term lesson is clear: unindexed wage floors turn price inflation into a silent pay cut for minimum wage earners.

segments.label: scene 41 (statement)
segments.text: Do you think statutory wage floors should be automatically tied to price inflation or left to legislative votes? Tell us in the comments.

segments.label: scene 42 (statement)
segments.text: Subscribe to Plotline Data for more clear, data-driven insights into the economic forces shaping daily life.
